tldr: We propose ReCo, a legged manipulation framework that trains an RL locomotion policy to have predictable response behavior for Model Predictive Control (MPC), enabling highly accurate end-effector tracking while walking.
hero_caption: Overall architecture of ReCo. A locomotion policy is trained with response shaping to be well-behaved, its closed-loop dynamics are identified, and MPC incorporating this response model jointly optimizes locomotion commands to the base and arm joint velocities.
overview:
Legged manipulation—mounting a robotic arm on a quadruped robot—is a promising technology for working in rough terrain. However, performing millimeter-precision manipulation while walking is challenging: every footstep shakes the base in heave and pitch, causing large tracking errors at the end-effector.

A popular direction combines reinforcement learning (RL), which excels at rough-terrain locomotion, with model predictive control (MPC), which excels at handling constraints and trajectory tracking. However, this approach hits a major wall. For MPC to coordinate the arm and legs effectively, it must accurately predict how the base will move given a locomotion command. In standard RL policies, command response varies widely with gait phase, contact conditions, and arm swinging.

To address this, the authors turned the problem on its head: why not train the RL policy to be predictable (response-consistent) for MPC? This led to the proposed framework, ReCo. First, the RL policy is trained with response shaping rewards so that its transient response to commands and gait-cycle oscillations are consistent. Next, this behavior is identified as a low-order response model plus a harmonic Fourier series and embedded into MPC's internal prediction model. As a result, MPC anticipates locomotion lag and periodic base oscillations, allowing the arm to proactively cancel them out while tracking the end-effector trajectory.

Across 50 challenging tracking trajectories in simulation, ReCo reduced end-effector position RMSE by 28.7% and orientation RMSE by 27.4% compared to the best baseline for each metric. Furthermore, using a real Unitree Go2 with an ARX X5 arm, fully onboard continuous legged manipulation—such as tidying cardboard boxes and opening a cabinet door while walking—was demonstrated on a Jetson Orin NX.
contributions: Introduced response shaping rewards that improve transient response repeatability and gait-cycle oscillation regularity, establishing a way to train an RL locomotion policy that is predictable for MPC.

Built a framework that embeds the identified closed-loop response model and gait-cycle oscillation model into MPC to jointly optimize base velocity commands and arm joint velocities for world-frame end-effector tracking.
Reduced position RMSE by 28.7% and orientation RMSE by 27.4% on a simulation benchmark, and demonstrated fully onboard continuous legged manipulation while walking on hardware.

sections.heading: Why Working While Walking Is Hard, and the Idea of a Predictable Policy
sections.summary: In manipulation while walking, every footstep perturbation propagates to the end-effector. In conventional hybrid RL-MPC setups, the bottleneck is MPC's inability to predict policy response variations. This paper proposes a new solution: train the policy to be predictable.
sections.details:
Mounting a robotic arm on a quadruped robot allows it to traverse steps and rough terrain to perform inspections and tool use. However, unlike traditional mobile manipulation where the base stops before the arm moves, continuous legged manipulation—tracking a world-frame end-effector trajectory while walking—is extremely difficult. With every footstep, the base's position, tilt, and gait-induced periodic vibrations shake the arm's base, leading to large errors at the end-effector.

From a control perspective, stable locomotion and precise manipulation demand conflicting properties. Reinforcement learning (RL) excels at robust locomotion under disturbances, but tuning whole-body RL to achieve both end-effector accuracy and walking stability within a single reward function is very difficult. On the other hand, model-based MPC handles end-effector tracking and constraints well, but accurately modeling complex foot-contact dynamics on rough terrain is notoriously hard.

A promising modular approach leaves locomotion stabilization to RL and lets a higher-level MPC coordinate the base and arm. However, this encounters a fundamental issue: interface unpredictability. From the MPC perspective, the RL-controlled base is an unknown black box. Even when given a commanded velocity, how and when the base actually moves varies each time depending on gait phase, contact states, and arm weight. While a constant delay could be compensated with feedforward control, fluctuating delays and oscillations cannot be canceled.

The core insight of this work is that a locomotion policy should not merely be robust; it should also be predictable to the planner (MPC) commanding it. To make the division of labor work—where the base handles large displacements and the arm makes quick, fine adjustments within its workspace—the authors developed ReCo. It shapes the policy's response so it can be approximated by a low-order model, and embeds that predictive model directly into MPC.

captions.F1: Continuous legged manipulation on the real robot. With ReCo, the robot performs tasks such as tidying cardboard boxes, opening a cabinet door, and pick-and-place with high precision while continuing to walk.

sections.heading: The Evolution of Model-Based, Whole-Body RL, and Hybrid Control
sections.summary: Legged manipulation approaches span model-based control, whole-body RL, and hybrid methods combining both. ReCo falls under hybrid control, but sets itself apart by actively shaping and modeling the lower-level policy's response characteristics for the high-level planner.
sections.details:
Related work falls broadly into three categories.

### Model-Based Legged Manipulation
Methods using ground reaction force optimization and whole-body MPC (such as ALMA and perceptive MPC) explicitly optimize base and arm motions based on robot kinematic and dynamic models. While they naturally handle obstacle avoidance and geometric constraints, modeling errors accumulate under unknown rough terrain and slippery contact conditions, often leading to locomotion failure.

### Learning-Based Locomotion and Manipulation
Large-scale simulation training with domain randomization has yielded many RL locomotion policies that effortlessly traverse harsh terrain. Some studies extend these to whole-body manipulation (e.g., Deep WBC, RoboDuet, UMI on Legs). However, optimizing task-space end-effector accuracy and fall prevention within a single policy limits generalization when given arbitrary 3D end-effector trajectories not seen during training.

### Hybrid Control and Policy Response Modeling
Hybrid control combining RL's robustness and MPC's flexibility has also been explored. For example, prior work (Ma et al.) predicted the wrench exerted on the base by arm motion using a model-based planner and fed it into an RL locomotion policy to resist arm reaction forces. However, even with this, the MPC did not accurately know how the base would move in response to its locomotion commands. ReCo inverts and advances this relationship: it trains the policy response itself into an identifiable form, allowing MPC to incorporate that closed-loop model into trajectory planning, which is the decisive novelty.

sections.heading: Training a Predictable Policy and Embedding Its Identified Model into MPC
sections.summary: ReCo consists of three stages: training an RL locomotion policy with response shaping rewards, identifying closed-loop responses via low-order models and gait-cycle Fourier series, and jointly optimizing joint velocities and base commands with policy-aware MPC.
sections.details:
ReCo's overall architecture is divided into three main components: response shaping training, closed-loop response identification, and policy-aware MPC.

### Problem Formulation (III-A)
Given a reference end-effector pose trajectory in the world frame $T_{WE}^{\mathrm{ref}}(t) \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$, the goal is to track it while the robot keeps walking. The control inputs MPC solves for are the command vector to the locomotion policy $\mathbf{c} = (c_x, c_y, c_\omega, c_h, c_\theta) \in \mathbb{R}^5$ (forward and lateral velocity, yaw rate, base height, and pitch angle) and joint velocity commands for the 6-DoF arm $u_q \in \mathbb{R}^6$.

### Response-Consistent Locomotion Learning (III-B)
The policy is trained with Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO), adding response shaping terms to the standard locomotion rewards. Penalties are imposed to guide the transient response toward a critically damped second-order reference generator when commands change. Here, the periodic gait-induced oscillation component $\hat{\delta}(\phi, \nu)$ is estimated via running average and subtracted, ensuring that only the transient response cleanly tracks the reference. Furthermore, an across-domain consistency loss sends identical command sequences to parallel environments with randomized base mass, friction, and actuator strengths, penalizing response differences among them. This produces a policy that responds with consistent delay and behavior even under disturbances and shifting dynamics.

### Closed-Loop Response Model Identification (III-C)
The trained policy's behavior is formulated mathematically for MPC computation. The velocity channels (forward, lateral, yaw) are modeled as first-order lag systems to keep computational cost low. In contrast, base height $z$, pitch $\theta$, and roll $\rho$—which directly affect end-effector height and orientation—are modeled by combining a first-order command response with a harmonic Fourier series (up to 2nd harmonics) dependent on gait phase $\phi$ and velocity. Parameters are identified via nonlinear least squares using offline data generated by feeding step and chirp commands to the trained policy.

### Policy-Aware Model Predictive Control (III-D)
The identified base response model is coupled with arm kinematics, defining a cost function that considers end-effector pose error, joint limits, and self-collision avoidance. This is solved in real time at 100 Hz using SQP (Sequential Quadratic Programming) via the OCS2 toolbox. Because MPC's prediction horizon fully accounts for how much the base lags behind commands and how much it oscillates upon contact, the arm can proactively move to cancel out base oscillations.

(B) Its closed-loop response characteristics are system-identified into a low-order model. (C) MPC incorporating this response model jointly derives locomotion commands and arm commands to minimize end-effector tracking error.

sections.heading: Superior Tracking Accuracy and Robustness Validated in Sim and Real
sections.summary: On a benchmark of 50 challenging trajectories over undulating terrain, ReCo reduced position error by 28.7% and orientation error by 27.4% relative to the best baselines. Ablations confirmed the synergy of response shaping and model identification, and real-world fully onboard operation was validated.
sections.details:
To evaluate the method, extensive experiments were conducted using a Unitree Go2 equipped with a 6-DoF ARX X5 arm.

### Benchmark Evaluation (IV-A, IV-B)
Undulating terrain with height variations of $\pm 0.10$ m was created in simulation (MuJoCo), along with 50 end-effector trajectories featuring varied geometries and velocity profiles that extend beyond the arm's workspace. For each controller, 100 runs were evaluated: 50 nominal runs and 50 disturbance runs with an 80 N, 0.1 s external force impulse (8 Ns impulse) applied at the base center of mass. Comparisons included whole-body MPC (Pure MPC), a wrench-predictive hybrid method (Ma et al.), and recent whole-body RL methods (RoboDuet, Visual WBC, UMI on Legs).

The results were compelling. ReCo reduced position RMSE by 28.7% compared to the best baseline (Pure MPC) and orientation RMSE by 27.4% compared to the best baseline (Ma et al.). Task success rate (neither falling nor exceeding terminal and path error tolerances) reached 75/100 for ReCo, whereas the strongest baseline, RoboDuet+PP, managed only 42/100; ReCo also had the fewest falls among all methods. Under external force impulses, position error increased by only 3.4% relative to nominal runs (compared to 6.4% for Ma et al.), demonstrating strong disturbance rejection.

### Ablation Studies and Prediction Accuracy (IV-C, IV-D, IV-E)
A $2\times 2$ factorial ablation analyzed the roles of response shaping and model identification. Without response shaping, position RMSE was 0.257 m, but adding shaping alone improved it by 35.4% to 0.166 m. Adding the identified model into MPC brought it further to 0.135 m (an additional 18.7% improvement). On unseen command data, response shaping reduced base velocity prediction mean squared error (MSE) by 59.6%. Moreover, when the arm moved vigorously, the residual RMS of base forward velocity worsened by 0.0210 m/s for the unshaped policy, but increased by only 0.0040 m/s for the shaped policy.

Incorporating the gait-cycle oscillation model (Equation 7) improved end-effector height prediction RMSE from 6.49 mm to 3.58 mm (a 44.8% improvement), significantly reducing vertical oscillation errors in the 1.5–8 Hz trotting band.

### Hardware Experiments (IV-F)
A Jetson Orin NX was mounted on the real Go2 + X5 arm, running the full system onboard via ROS 2. Computational load averaged 75% CPU and 43% memory, running comfortably in real time. Across 8 trajectories tracked in a motion capture environment, the robot achieved an average position RMSE of 0.0760 m and orientation RMSE of $9.93^\circ$. In non-mocap settings, the robot stably performed VR-teleoperated box tidying, cabinet door opening, and pick-and-place tasks while continuously walking.

sections.heading: Summary and Next Steps: Modular Control Enabled by Predictability
sections.summary: ReCo achieves high-precision continuous legged manipulation by training a locomotion policy to be predictable and embedding its model into MPC. Future directions include modeling coupled arm-base dynamics more strictly and extending to vision-guided locomotion.
sections.details:
This paper presented ReCo, a novel legged manipulation framework coupling response-consistent locomotion learning with policy-aware MPC. Both simulation and real-world experiments showed that end-effector tracking accuracy can be substantially improved while maintaining walking stability.

The authors also candidly discuss limitations and future extensions. First, while model identification dramatically reduced position tracking error, orientation RMSE showed a slight increase. This is likely because the current response model treats channels independently, neglecting some of the coupled translation-rotation dynamics. Second, response repeatability along the height dimension did not improve as much as horizontal velocity, suggesting room for better reward design.

Future work includes incorporating the arm motion's effect on the base more precisely into the closed-loop response model and extending this predictive interface to rough-terrain adaptive locomotion policies that use visual inputs such as cameras.

takeaways: When pairing an RL policy with model-based control (MPC), training the policy to exhibit predictable behavior for the MPC (response shaping) is highly effective.
Modeling gait-induced base oscillations as a velocity-dependent Fourier series allows the arm to cancel out locomotion vibrations in a feedforward manner.
Jointly optimizing base locomotion commands and arm joint velocities for world-frame end-effector trajectories via MPC yields accuracy far superior to uncoordinated, separate trackers.
limitations: While model identification substantially reduced end-effector position error, orientation RMSE worsened slightly, indicating that coupled translational and rotational dynamics are not fully captured.
Despite including a height term in the across-domain consistency loss, repeatability improvements in the height channel were limited compared to horizontal velocities.
In real-world non-mocap evaluations, onboard odometry drift could not be completely isolated from the tracking error metrics.
